NOTICE OF BELIEF OF ABANDONMENT (REAL PROPERTY) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan Lee

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet addresses California's statutory Notice of Belief of Abandonment procedure for real property leased by Jordan Lee from Acme Properties, LLC at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814. That procedure — set out in Civil Code § 1951.3 for real property other than commercial real property, and in the separate, parallel Civil Code § 1951.35 for commercial real property — lets a lessor who reasonably believes a lessee has abandoned leased real property give written notice that, if the lessee does not respond in the manner and within the time the statute specifies, causes the real property to be deemed abandoned and the lease to terminate. It is a distinct statutory mechanism from an unlawful detainer notice to pay rent or quit under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 1161–1162, and from the separate statute governing disposition of a departed tenant's personal property left behind after a tenancy has already ended — this document does not address either of those. This document states California statutory law as of the date signed below. It does not determine that any specific lessee has abandoned any specific property, does not determine that any particular belief of abandonment was reasonable, and does not determine whether 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 is or is not "commercial real property" within the meaning of the statute.

GENERAL EFFECT OF AN UNREBUTTED NOTICE
Under Civil Code § 1951.3(b), real property is deemed abandoned by the lessee, within the meaning of Civil Code § 1951.2, and the lease terminates, if the lessor gives written notice of belief of abandonment as the statute provides and the lessee fails to give the lessor written notice — before the date of termination stated in the lessor's notice — both stating that the lessee does not intend to abandon the property and stating an address at which the lessee may be served by certified mail in an unlawful detainer action. This is a conditional, self-executing statutory consequence: the deemed-abandonment and lease termination follow automatically from the lessee's failure to respond in the specified way, not from any separate adjudication at the time the notice is given.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "Real property shall be deemed abandoned by the lessee, within the meaning of Section 1951.2, and the lease shall terminate if the lessor gives written notice of belief of abandonment as provided in this section and the lessee fails to give the lessor written notice, prior to the date of termination specified in the lessor’s notice, stating that the lessee does not intend to abandon the real property and stating an address at which the lessee may be served by certified mail in any action for unlawful detainer of the real property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, general rule on deemed abandonment and lease termination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.3.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the general rule of subdivision (b). It does not state the separate conditions in subdivision (c) that make giving the notice available in the first place, the delivery rules in subdivision (d), the required form in subdivision (e), or the four statutory grounds in subdivision (f) on which a lessee can prevent the property from being deemed abandoned even after an unrebutted notice — each addressed in other clauses of this document. Subdivision (b) itself does not define "written notice" from the lessee beyond the two things that notice must state, and this document does not address what form a lessee's responsive notice must take beyond the statute's own words.

SCOPE AND THRESHOLD CONDITIONS (NON-COMMERCIAL REAL PROPERTY)
Civil Code § 1951.3(a) states that this section applies to real property other than commercial real property, as defined in Civil Code § 1954.26(d). For that non-commercial real property, § 1951.3(c) permits the lessor to give a notice of belief of abandonment only where the rent on the property has been due and unpaid for at least 14 consecutive days and the lessor reasonably believes that the lessee has abandoned the property. Both conditions — the 14-consecutive-day unpaid-rent period and the lessor's reasonable belief of abandonment — must be present before this particular notice procedure is available for this category of property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "This section applies to real property other than commercial real property, as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 1954.26."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, scope limited to non-commercial real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.3.)
  "The lessor may give a notice of belief of abandonment to the lessee pursuant to this section only where the rent on the property has been due and unpaid for at least 14 consecutive days and the lessor reasonably believes that the lessee has abandoned the property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, 14-day unpaid rent and reasonable belief threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.3.)
  Known gap: This clause covers only the threshold conditions for real property that is not "commercial real property" as Civil Code § 1954.26(d) defines that term; the parallel statute for commercial real property, Civil Code § 1951.35, sets a different threshold (tied to the lease's own rent-default period, with a 3-day floor rather than a fixed 14 days) and is addressed in a separate clause of this document. Section 1951.3(c) does not itself define "reasonably believes," and this document does not determine whether any specific lessor's belief in any specific case was reasonable — subdivision (f)(2), addressed elsewhere in this document, separately provides that a lessor's mere knowledge that the lessee left personal property behind does not by itself defeat reasonableness, but that is a limited negative rule, not an affirmative definition of what makes a belief reasonable.

WHAT COUNTS AS "COMMERCIAL REAL PROPERTY"
Civil Code § 1954.26(d) defines "commercial real property" — the term that determines whether § 1951.3 or the separate § 1951.35 governs a notice of belief of abandonment — to include any part, portion, or unit of real property and any related facilities, space, or services, except four listed categories: a dwelling or dwelling unit subject to Civil Code § 1940; an accommodation in a residential hotel as defined in Health and Safety Code § 50519, or comparable accommodations specifically regulated by a public entity in structures where 20 percent or more of the accommodations are occupied as a primary residence; certain hotel units in structures meeting a similar occupancy and rent-control history threshold as of August 5, 1987; and any space or dwelling unit in a mobilehome park as defined in Health and Safety Code § 18214.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "“Commercial real property” includes any part, portion, or unit thereof, and any related facilities, space, or services, except the following:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.26(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, definition of "commercial real property" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.26.)
  "(1) Any dwelling or dwelling unit subject to the provisions of Section 1940."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.26(d)(1)-(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the four excluded (non-commercial) categories (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.26.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (d)'s definition of "commercial real property," the term dispositive of which of the two parallel abandonment-notice statutes applies. It does not quote or independently verify the cross-referenced definitions in Civil Code § 1940, Health and Safety Code § 50519, or Health and Safety Code § 18214, which subdivision (d) itself relies on; a determination of whether a specific property falls within one of the four excluded categories may turn on those other statutes' own text, which this document does not state.

HOW THE NOTICE MUST BE DELIVERED
For non-commercial real property, Civil Code § 1951.3(d) requires that the lessor's notice of belief of abandonment be personally delivered to the lessee or sent by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to the lessee's last known address, and — if there is reason to believe the notice sent to that address will not be received by the lessee — also sent to any other address known to the lessor where the lessee may reasonably be expected to receive it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "The lessor’s notice of belief of abandonment shall be personally delivered to the lessee or sent by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to the lessee at the lessee’s last known address and, if there is reason to believe that the notice sent to that address will not be received by the lessee, also to any other address known to the lessor where the lessee may reasonably be expected to receive the notice."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, delivery methods for non-commercial real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.3.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the delivery methods available for the non-commercial-property notice under § 1951.3(d). The parallel commercial-property statute, § 1951.35(d), authorizes an additional delivery method (a recognized overnight carrier) not available under § 1951.3(d), addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document does not determine, for any specific case, whether a lessor had "reason to believe" a notice would not be received at a given address, which is a factual determination the statute leaves unaddressed beyond its own words.

MINIMUM TIME BEFORE THE STATED TERMINATION DATE
Civil Code § 1951.3(c) requires that the date of termination of the lease be specified in the lessor's notice, and that this date be not less than 15 days after the notice is served personally, or, if the notice is mailed, not less than 18 days after the notice is deposited in the mail.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "The date of termination of the lease shall be specified in the lessor’s notice and shall be not less than 15 days after the notice is served personally or, if mailed, not less than 18 days after the notice is deposited in the mail."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, minimum time before the stated termination date (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.3.)
  Known gap: These are minimums fixed by this one statute for non-commercial real property; the notice must state a termination date at least this far out, but nothing in this clause addresses whether a lessor may or must state a later date, and this document does not calculate any specific termination date for any specific notice. The parallel commercial-property statute uses a single 15-day minimum regardless of delivery method (addressed in a separate clause), which is a different rule from the mail-based 18-day minimum stated here.

STATUTORY GROUNDS THAT DEFEAT DEEMED ABANDONMENT
Civil Code § 1951.3(f) provides that the real property shall not be deemed abandoned under this section if the lessee proves any of four things: that at the time the notice was given, the rent was not in fact due and unpaid for 14 consecutive days; that at the time the notice was given, it was not reasonable for the lessor to believe the lessee had abandoned the property — and the statute adds that the lessor's mere knowledge that the lessee left personal property on the property does not, of itself, justify a finding that the lessor's belief was unreasonable; that before the date specified in the lessor's notice, the lessee gave the lessor written notice of intent not to abandon the property along with a certified-mail service address; or that during the period beginning 14 days before the notice was given and ending on the date the lease would otherwise have terminated, the lessee paid the lessor all or part of the unpaid rent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "The fact that the lessor knew that the lessee left personal property on the real property does not, of itself, justify a finding that the lessor did not reasonably believe that the lessee had abandoned the real property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the four statutory grounds defeating deemed abandonment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.3.)
  "During the period beginning 14 days before the time the notice of belief of abandonment was given and ending on the date the lease would have terminated pursuant to the notice, the lessee paid to the lessor all or a portion of the rent due and unpaid on the real property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(f)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the rent-payment-during-the-window ground (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.3.)
  Known gap: Subdivision (f) places the burden of proving each of these grounds on the lessee, and this document does not determine whether any specific lessee has proved, or could prove, any of them in any specific case. The fourth ground (partial or full rent payment during the specified window) does not by its own terms say whether it requires payment sufficient to cure the full 14-day delinquency or merely some payment during that window; this document states the statute's own "all or a portion of" language without resolving that ambiguity.

RELATIONSHIP TO OTHER NOTICES AND PROCEEDINGS
Civil Code § 1951.3(g) states that nothing in the section precludes the lessor or the lessee from otherwise proving that the real property has been abandoned by the lessee within the meaning of § 1951.2 — that is, the statutory notice procedure is one way to establish abandonment, not the exclusive way. Section 1951.3(h) separately states that nothing in the section precludes the lessor from serving a notice requiring the lessee to pay rent or quit under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 1161 and 1162 at any time those sections permit, and that giving the notice of belief of abandonment does not satisfy the requirements of those sections.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "Nothing in this section precludes the lessor or the lessee from otherwise proving that the real property has been abandoned by the lessee within the meaning of Section 1951.2."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(g) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, notice procedure is not the exclusive way to prove abandonment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.3.)
  "The giving of the notice provided by this section does not satisfy the requirements of Sections 1161 and 1162 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(h) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, does not substitute for a pay-rent-or-quit notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.3.)
  Known gap: This clause establishes only that the two procedures are legally independent and that one does not substitute for the other; it does not address the separate statute at Civil Code § 1991, which permits — but does not require — combining a notice of belief of abandonment with a related notice concerning a departed tenant's personal property left on the premises, a topic addressed in this corpus's separate document on disposition of abandoned personal property, not in this document. This document does not determine which procedure, or combination of procedures, is applicable or advisable in any specific case.

THE PARALLEL PROCEDURE FOR COMMERCIAL REAL PROPERTY
Civil Code § 1951.35, added effective January 1, 2019 by the same legislation that limited § 1951.3 to non-commercial real property, applies only to commercial real property as defined in § 1954.26(d) and sets a different threshold for when a lessor may give the notice: the rent must have been due and unpaid for at least the number of days required for the lessor to declare a rent default under the terms of the lease, but in no case less than three days, and the lessor must reasonably believe the lessee has abandoned the property. Unlike the non-commercial statute's split 15-day/18-day timing, § 1951.35(c) requires the stated termination date to be not less than 15 days after the notice is served personally, sent by an overnight courier service, or deposited in the mail — a single 15-day minimum regardless of delivery method. Section 1951.35(d) also permits delivery by a recognized overnight carrier, an option § 1951.3(d) does not include for non-commercial real property. The commercial statute's rebuttal grounds, exclusivity language, and relationship to Code of Civil Procedure §§ 1161–1162 in § 1951.35(f)–(h) otherwise track the non-commercial statute's structure, adjusted for the lease-default-based timing rather than the fixed 14-day period.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "The lessor may give notice of belief of abandonment pursuant to this section only if the rent on the property has been due and unpaid for at least the number of days required for the lessor to declare a rent default under the terms of the lease, but in no case less than three days, and the lessor reasonably believes that the lessee has abandoned the property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.35(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, commercial real property scope and threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.35.)
  "The lessor’s notice of belief of abandonment shall be personally delivered to the lessee, sent by a recognized overnight carrier, or sent by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to the lessee at the lessee’s last known address"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.35(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, commercial-property delivery methods including overnight carrier (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.35.)
  Known gap: This clause summarizes § 1951.35's points of difference from § 1951.3 rather than quoting the commercial statute's rebuttal-grounds subdivision (f) in full; a lessor or lessee dealing with commercial real property should consult § 1951.35's own complete text rather than this comparative summary. Published California case law construing a notice of belief of abandonment for a commercial lease — 250 L.L.C. v. Photopoint Corp. (USA), 131 Cal. App. 4th 703 (2005), and Avalon Pacific-Santa Ana, L.P. v. HD Supply Repair & Remodel, LLC, 192 Cal. App. 4th 1183 (2011) — was decided before § 1951.35 existed, when a single, undifferentiated § 1951.3 governed both commercial and non-commercial property; this document does not treat that pre-2019 case law as authority for how a court would apply the current, commercial-property-specific § 1951.35.

FILLABLE TEXT — NOTICE OF BELIEF OF ABANDONMENT (NON-COMMERCIAL REAL PROPERTY)
NOTICE OF BELIEF OF ABANDONMENT

To: Jordan Lee (Name of lessee/tenant)
_____________________________ (Address of lessee/tenant)

This notice is given pursuant to Section 1951.3 of the Civil Code concerning the real property leased by you at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 (state location of the property by address or other sufficient description). The rent on this property has been due and unpaid for 14 consecutive days and the lessor/landlord believes that you have abandoned the property.

The real property will be deemed abandoned within the meaning of Section 1951.2 of the Civil Code and your lease will terminate on September 25, 2026 (a date not less than 15 days after this notice is served personally, or, if mailed, not less than 18 days after this notice is deposited in the mail) unless before that date the lessor/landlord receives at the address indicated below a written notice from you stating both of the following: (1) Your intent not to abandon the real property. (2) An address at which you may be served by certified mail in any action for unlawful detainer of the real property.

You are required to pay the rent due and unpaid on this real property as required by the lease, and your failure to do so can lead to a court proceeding against you.

Dated: September 7, 2026

_____________________________ (Signature of lessor/landlord)
Acme Properties, LLC (Type or print name of lessor/landlord)
123 Main St., Suite 100, Sacramento, CA 95814 (Address to which lessee/tenant is to send notice)

This form uses the wording Civil Code § 1951.3(e) itself sets out for real property other than commercial real property; it is not the form for commercial real property, addressed in a separate clause of this document.

FILLABLE TEXT — NOTICE OF BELIEF OF ABANDONMENT (COMMERCIAL REAL PROPERTY)
NOTICE OF BELIEF OF ABANDONMENT

To: Jordan Lee (Name of lessee/tenant)
_____________________________ (Address of lessee/tenant)

This notice is given pursuant to Section 1951.35 of the Civil Code concerning the real property leased by you at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 (state location of the property by address or other sufficient description). The rent on this property has been due and unpaid for the number of days necessary to declare a rent default under your lease and the lessor/landlord believes that you have abandoned the property.

The real property will be deemed abandoned within the meaning of Section 1951.2 of the Civil Code and your lease will terminate on September 25, 2026 (a date not less than 15 days after this notice is served personally, sent by overnight courier service, or deposited in the mail) unless before that date the lessor/landlord receives at the address below a written notice from you stating both of the following: (1) Your intent not to abandon the real property. (2) An address at which you may be served by certified mail in any action for unlawful detainer of real property.

You are required to pay the rent due and unpaid on this real property as required by the lease, and your failure to do so can lead to a court proceeding against you.

Dated: September 7, 2026

_____________________________ (Signature of lessor/landlord)
Acme Properties, LLC (Type or print name of lessor/landlord)
123 Main St., Suite 100, Sacramento, CA 95814 (Address to which lessee/tenant is to send notice)

This form uses the wording Civil Code § 1951.35(e) itself sets out for commercial real property only; it is not the form for non-commercial real property, addressed in a separate clause of this document. Whether 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 is "commercial real property" within the meaning of Civil Code § 1954.26(d) determines which of the two forms in this document applies — this document does not make that determination.

RECORDKEEPING WORKSHEET AND DECLARATION OF SERVICE
RECORDKEEPING WORKSHEET — 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814. Landlord/lessor: Acme Properties, LLC. Tenant/lessee: Jordan Lee. Rent unpaid since (date): August 10, 2026. Date of this notice: September 7, 2026. Termination date stated in notice: September 25, 2026.

This worksheet is a recordkeeping aid only. It does not determine that the property described above is or is not "commercial real property," does not determine that any period of unpaid rent or any belief of abandonment satisfies the applicable statute, and does not constitute legal advice.

Declaration of Service. This notice was served on Jordan Lee on _______________ (date), by the following method (check one): ☐ personal delivery to the lessee; ☐ first-class mail, postage prepaid, to the lessee's last known address; ☐ (commercial real property only) a recognized overnight carrier; ☐ mailed to an additional address under Civil Code § 1951.3(d) or § 1951.35(d) because there was reason to believe the primary address would not reach the lessee.

Served by: _______________ (name) Date: _______________

Executed on September 7, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Acme Properties, LLC: _______________________ Date: _______________

expectedJSON.gap: These are minimums fixed by this one statute for non-commercial real property; the notice must state a termination date at least this far out, but nothing in this clause addresses whether a lessor may or must state a later date, and this document does not calculate any specific termination date for any specific notice. The parallel commercial-property statute uses a single 15-day minimum regardless of delivery method (addressed in a separate clause), which is a different rule from the mail-based 18-day minimum stated here.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 1951.3(f) provides that the real property shall not be deemed abandoned under this section if the lessee proves any of four things: that at the time the notice was given, the rent was not in fact due and unpaid for 14 consecutive days; that at the time the notice was given, it was not reasonable for the lessor to believe the lessee had abandoned the property — and the statute adds that the lessor's mere knowledge that the lessee left personal property on the property does not, of itself, justify a finding that the lessor's belief was unreasonable; that before the date specified in the lessor's notice, the lessee gave the lessor written notice of intent not to abandon the property along with a certified-mail service address; or that during the period beginning 14 days before the notice was given and ending on the date the lease would otherwise have terminated, the lessee paid the lessor all or part of the unpaid rent.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the four statutory grounds defeating deemed abandonment
citations.quote: The fact that the lessor knew that the lessee left personal property on the real property does not, of itself, justify a finding that the lessor did not reasonably believe that the lessee had abandoned the real property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(f)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the rent-payment-during-the-window ground
citations.quote: During the period beginning 14 days before the time the notice of belief of abandonment was given and ending on the date the lease would have terminated pursuant to the notice, the lessee paid to the lessor all or a portion of the rent due and unpaid on the real property.

expectedJSON.gap: Subdivision (f) places the burden of proving each of these grounds on the lessee, and this document does not determine whether any specific lessee has proved, or could prove, any of them in any specific case. The fourth ground (partial or full rent payment during the specified window) does not by its own terms say whether it requires payment sufficient to cure the full 14-day delinquency or merely some payment during that window; this document states the statute's own "all or a portion of" language without resolving that ambiguity.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 1951.3(g) states that nothing in the section precludes the lessor or the lessee from otherwise proving that the real property has been abandoned by the lessee within the meaning of § 1951.2 — that is, the statutory notice procedure is one way to establish abandonment, not the exclusive way. Section 1951.3(h) separately states that nothing in the section precludes the lessor from serving a notice requiring the lessee to pay rent or quit under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 1161 and 1162 at any time those sections permit, and that giving the notice of belief of abandonment does not satisfy the requirements of those sections.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, notice procedure is not the exclusive way to prove abandonment
citations.quote: Nothing in this section precludes the lessor or the lessee from otherwise proving that the real property has been abandoned by the lessee within the meaning of Section 1951.2.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, does not substitute for a pay-rent-or-quit notice
citations.quote: The giving of the notice provided by this section does not satisfy the requirements of Sections 1161 and 1162 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause establishes only that the two procedures are legally independent and that one does not substitute for the other; it does not address the separate statute at Civil Code § 1991, which permits — but does not require — combining a notice of belief of abandonment with a related notice concerning a departed tenant's personal property left on the premises, a topic addressed in this corpus's separate document on disposition of abandoned personal property, not in this document. This document does not determine which procedure, or combination of procedures, is applicable or advisable in any specific case.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 1951.35, added effective January 1, 2019 by the same legislation that limited § 1951.3 to non-commercial real property, applies only to commercial real property as defined in § 1954.26(d) and sets a different threshold for when a lessor may give the notice: the rent must have been due and unpaid for at least the number of days required for the lessor to declare a rent default under the terms of the lease, but in no case less than three days, and the lessor must reasonably believe the lessee has abandoned the property. Unlike the non-commercial statute's split 15-day/18-day timing, § 1951.35(c) requires the stated termination date to be not less than 15 days after the notice is served personally, sent by an overnight courier service, or deposited in the mail — a single 15-day minimum regardless of delivery method. Section 1951.35(d) also permits delivery by a recognized overnight carrier, an option § 1951.3(d) does not include for non-commercial real property. The commercial statute's rebuttal grounds, exclusivity language, and relationship to Code of Civil Procedure §§ 1161–1162 in § 1951.35(f)–(h) otherwise track the non-commercial statute's structure, adjusted for the lease-default-based timing rather than the fixed 14-day period.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.35(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, commercial real property scope and threshold
citations.quote: The lessor may give notice of belief of abandonment pursuant to this section only if the rent on the property has been due and unpaid for at least the number of days required for the lessor to declare a rent default under the terms of the lease, but in no case less than three days, and the lessor reasonably believes that the lessee has abandoned the property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.35(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, commercial-property delivery methods including overnight carrier
citations.quote: The lessor’s notice of belief of abandonment shall be personally delivered to the lessee, sent by a recognized overnight carrier, or sent by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to the lessee at the lessee’s last known address

expectedJSON.gap: This clause summarizes § 1951.35's points of difference from § 1951.3 rather than quoting the commercial statute's rebuttal-grounds subdivision (f) in full; a lessor or lessee dealing with commercial real property should consult § 1951.35's own complete text rather than this comparative summary. Published California case law construing a notice of belief of abandonment for a commercial lease — 250 L.L.C. v. Photopoint Corp. (USA), 131 Cal. App. 4th 703 (2005), and Avalon Pacific-Santa Ana, L.P. v. HD Supply Repair & Remodel, LLC, 192 Cal. App. 4th 1183 (2011) — was decided before § 1951.35 existed, when a single, undifferentiated § 1951.3 governed both commercial and non-commercial property; this document does not treat that pre-2019 case law as authority for how a court would apply the current, commercial-property-specific § 1951.35.
